phase1.intro:
Polymorphism literally means "many forms" — one name, different behavior depending on context. You've actually already met both flavors of it.

Which do you want to revisit first?

topics.buttonText: What's the difference between compile-time and runtime polymorphism?
dialogue: [[term:Compile-time polymorphism]] is method overloading — Calculator's three `add()` methods share a name but differ in parameters, and [[key:Java decides which one to call while compiling, based purely on what arguments you wrote]].

[[term:Runtime polymorphism]] is method overriding — `Animal myAnimal = new Dog();` then `myAnimal.makeSound()` runs Dog's version, and [[key:that decision happens while the program is actually running, based on the object's real type]].

stickyNote.flavor: 🕐 decided at compile time vs decided while running
stickyNote.definition: Compile-time polymorphism = overloading, resolved by argument types at compile time. Runtime polymorphism = overriding, resolved by actual object type at runtime.

topics.buttonText: What is upcasting, and what does it cost me?
dialogue: `Animal myAnimal = new Dog();` is called [[term:upcasting]] — treating a more specific object as its more general type — and Java does it automatically, no cast needed.
The tradeoff: [[warn:through an Animal-typed variable, you can only call methods Animal actually declares]] — `myAnimal.wagTail()` won't compile, even though the object underneath really is a Dog.

stickyNote.flavor: ⬆️ automatic, but you lose access to the subclass's extras
stickyNote.definition: Treating a subclass object as its superclass type, done automatically. Only the superclass's declared methods are callable through that reference.

topics.buttonText: How do I go back from Animal to Dog?
dialogue: Going the other direction is [[term:downcasting]] — converting back from Animal to Dog — and [[warn:this one you have to do explicitly with (Dog)]], because Java can't be sure at compile time it's actually safe.
That's exactly what `instanceof` is for: checking "is this really a Dog" BEFORE you downcast, so you never risk a crash.

stickyNote.flavor: ⬇️ explicit cast, checked first with instanceof
stickyNote.definition: Downcasting converts a superclass reference back to a subclass type, requiring an explicit cast like (Dog). instanceof checks safety beforehand.

phase1.openingDialogue: Polymorphism has two forms — overloading resolved at compile time, overriding resolved at runtime — plus upcasting and downcasting between types. 🎭

phase2.errorMessage:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ClassCastException: Dog cannot be cast to Cat
        at Test.main(Test.java:16)
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:ClassCastException — this is what happens when you downcast to the wrong type]]. `animal` genuinely holds a Dog object underneath, but the code tries to force it into a Cat reference. Java checks this at runtime and refuses, since a Dog object simply isn't a Cat, no matter what you cast it to.

[[key:The fix is always checking with instanceof before you downcast]]: `if (animal instanceof Cat) { Cat cat = (Cat) animal; }`. That way, the cast only ever runs once you've already confirmed it's safe — [[key:instanceof turns a possible runtime crash into a simple, controlled check]].

phase3.openingDialogue: One interface, many forms — that's polymorphism! 🎭

mcq.question:
Why should you check with instanceof before downcasting?

A) It makes the code run faster
B) It prevents a ClassCastException by confirming the object is actually that type first
C) instanceof is required by Java syntax rules
D) Downcasting is always illegal without it

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a Payment class with processPayment() method.
Create CreditCard and PayPal subclasses that override processPayment():
• CreditCard: prints "Processing credit card payment of $[amount]"
• PayPal: prints "Processing PayPal payment of $[amount]"

In main, create an array of Payment references with both types.
Loop through and call processPayment(100) on each.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: the instanceof-then-cast pattern you just wrote got its own shortcut in Java 16 — pattern matching for instanceof lets you write `if (animal instanceof Dog dog) { dog.wagTail(); }` in one line, combining the check and the cast. It's newer syntax for the exact same safety idea you just learned.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more shape-shifting thought before you go~
